newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mosenergo, no longer Russia bellwether, said cheap.
newsitem.headline: Mosenergo, no longer Russia bellwether, said cheap.

text.p: Shares in Moscow power company Mosenergo have lost their role as the market bellwether but dealers said Russia's biggest regional utility now looks cheap despite gloomy fundamentals.
Falls in first-quarter profits and output announced last week have further dented an image that has already been affected by narrow share price fluctuations and low trading volumes.
Traders say Mosenergo's size in the sector and large -- by Russian standards -- market capitalisation of $3.23 billion will ensure that it remains one of Russia's most liquid stocks.

But with the share already widely held by Western investors, dealers believe the price will be increasingly driven by company fundamentals. They note that it has failed to respond much to plans to issue a Eurobond.

"This isn't the sort of news which rocks the market... I don't think the shares will be able to gain more than five percent on this news... It means the best days of these shares are maybe already over," said UFG trader Igor Vain.

Mosenergo started to advance in February last year, leading the whole market higher. In this year's New Year rally it leapt to $1.63 on January 23 from $1.02 on December 31. But it has since drifted down to $1.25.

Mosenergo's fundamentals will be strongly influenced by the current restructuring of the electricity industry, especially of national power company Unified Energy System (UES) EESR.RTS, which owns 49 percent of Mosenergo, dealers and analysts said.

Analysts said the fall in Mosenergo output to 20.50 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity in the first quarter of this year from 22.30 billion a year earlier reflects company plans to cut supplies to the electricity wholesale market (FOREM) under the current tariff system.

"Apparently they are hinting that they are cutting supplies to the FOREM. The current tariffs are not high enough to cover costs, when you take into account non-payments," said an analyst at investment bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
When production falls, the drop in costs is proportionally less than the fall in production, so costs per unit of output rise in these circumstances, he said.

But a planned cut in nationwide tariffs to industrial customers this year of 13 percent, to be partly countered by a two to three percent rise in tariffs to households, could cause Mosenergo to lose up to five percent of revenues, he said.
It is still not clear exactly when these changes will come into effect.

"If the tariffs don't change, if the situation doesn't improve for them on the FOREM, these are not good figures. If they get the same figures for the first half, and they are unlikely to change, I will have another look at how much this company is worth," he said.

According to investment bank Renaissance Capital, Mosenergo had a net profit margin in 1996 of 23 percent -- one of the highest of any Russian power company, beaten only by the Volzhskaya power station with 32 percent.

For the first quarter, when net profit on a Russian accounting cash basis fell to 850 billion roubles from 1.00 trillion a year earlier while sales rose to 4.90 trillion from 3.60 trillion roubles, this ratio fell to 17.4 percent. On an accruals basis it would be 27.7 percent.
On the other hand, traders said Mosenergo shares had already fallen as much as they were likely to in comparison to other Russian blue chips, leading some to believe the price could recover.
Andrei Kukk, head of equity operations at broker Rinako Plus, said the potential for heavy selling in Mosenergo was now largely exhausted after its decline so far this year.

"It's quite possible that another 4.5 million shares will be sold but after that there will be no more sellers," he said. When Mosenergo was being most actively traded earlier this year, daily volume was typically five million shares.
A salesman at a Western bank said selling orders for Mosenergo seemed to have dried up over the last few days and Western investors already holding the stock were appearing as buyers.

And even on fundamentals there is some good news. As the company with the biggest number of household consumers of electricity and heating, Mosenergo will benefit in the long term from the rise in household tariffs, analysts said.
